paragraphs.text: SHAHID BILAL HASSAN, J- The present appeal, converted from a petition for leave to appeal (CPLA No.714-L of 2012), arises out of a suit for possession by way of pre-emption instituted by the appellants on 14.03.2007 in respect of land measuring 12 kanals situated in Khata No.18, Khatooni Nos.120 to 123, Chak No.85/NB, Tehsil and District Rahim Yar Khan, seeking to pre-empt a sale effected in favour of the respondent through a registered sale deed dated 21.11.2006. Upon completion of the pleadings, the learned trial Court framed issues on 31.10.2007 and fixed the matter for the evidence of the plaintiffs. The record reflects that the proceedings thereafter remained protracted on account of repeated adjournments arising from diverse causes, including non-availability of evidence, declaration of public holidays, strikes by the legal fraternity, transfer of the case from one Court to another, and on certain occasions the engagement of learned counsel elsewhere. It is also borne out from the order sheets that on more than one date the plaintiffs' witnesses were present and their attendance was duly marked, though their evidence could not be recorded for reasons not wholly attributable to the plaintiffs. Eventually, on 14.10.2009, the learned trial Court, invoking the provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C., closed the appellants’/ plaintiffs' right to adduce evidence and, there being no evidence in support of the claim, proceeded to dismiss the suit. The appellants thereafter filed an application for review under Order XLVII, C.P.C., seeking recall of the order dated 14.10.2009, which was dismissed on the ground that the impugned order was appealable and, therefore, not amenable to review. Aggrieved, the appellants preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, which too met dismissal on 17.11.2011. A Civil Revision filed before the Lahore High Court also failed and was dismissed vide judgment dated 07.03.2012, affirming the concurrent view of the Courts below. Leave having been granted by this Court, the present appeal calls into question the legality and propriety of the judgments passed by the High Court and the Courts subordinate thereto.

Learned counsel for the appellants contended that the learned trial Court acted without lawful authority in invoking the penal provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. and closing the appellants' right to adduce evidence. He submitted that the record clearly demonstrates that the adjournment immediately preceding the impugned order dated 14.10.2009 was occasioned by a strike, observed by the legal fraternity, and not at the request or default of the appellants. It was argued that several earlier adjournments had also occurred due to circumstances beyond the appellants' control, including public holidays, transfer of the case, leave of the Presiding Officer, and occasions where the appellants' witnesses were present but their evidence could not be recorded. According to the learned counsel, the statutory precondition for invoking Order XVII Rule 3, CPC, namely that time had been granted at the request of the defaulting party, was altogether absent. He further argued that although the appellants initially sought review of the order dated 14.10.2009, the review was maintainable because the impugned order suffered from an error apparent on the face of the record inasmuch as a jurisdiction not vested in the trial Court had been exercised.

Conversely, learned counsel for the respondents supported the concurrent findings of the Courts below and submitted that the appellants had been afforded repeated opportunities extending over a considerable period to produce their evidence but failed to avail the same. It was contended that the learned trial Court rightly exercised its discretion under Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. to prevent unnecessary continuation of the proceedings. Learned counsel further submitted that once the order dated 14.10.2009 was appealable, the appellants could not invoke the review jurisdiction and, having elected to pursue that remedy, could not subsequently assail its dismissal. He, therefore, prayed for dismissal of the appeal.

In view of the rival submissions, the following question arises for determination: Whether, in the facts and circumstances of the present case, the learned trial Court lawfully invoked Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. to close the appellants' right to adduce evidence, and if not, whether the review petition preferred against the said order was maintainable notwithstanding the availability of an appellate remedy?
We have heard the learned counsel for the parties and have examined the record with their able assistance.

At the very outset we observe that Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. is a penal provision. It deprives a litigant of the valuable right to produce evidence and authorizes the Court to proceed with the suit notwithstanding the default of the party to whom time had earlier been granted. Being penal in nature, its application is conditioned upon strict compliance with the statutory requirements and cannot be resorted to mechanically. The Supreme Court has consistently held that the provision must receive strict construction before a litigant is visited with its adverse consequences.

The sequence of proceedings assumes considerable significance. The record reveals that numerous adjournments were occasioned by factors wholly unconnected with the conduct of the appellants, including declaration of public holidays, transfer of the case from one Court to another, leave of the Presiding Officer and strikes observed by the legal fraternity. More importantly, on more than one occasion the appellants' witnesses were present and their attendance was duly marked, yet their evidence could not be recorded. The order sheet unambiguously records that the proceedings could not continue because the legal fraternity was observing a strike. The matter was consequently adjourned to 14.10.2009. It is, therefore, beyond dispute that the adjournment immediately preceding the impugned order was neither sought by nor granted at the request of the appellants. In such circumstances, the indispensable condition for invoking Order XVII Rule 3 CPC, that time had been granted to the defaulting party for performing an act necessary for the progress of the suit, stood conspicuously absent.

This precise question is no longer res integra. In Qutab-ud-Din v. Gulzar (PLD 1991 SC 1109), this Court categorically held that where the previous adjournment was not granted on the request of the plaintiff, Order XVII Rule 3 CPC could not be invoked for closing the plaintiff's evidence. The Court observed that since the suit had not been adjourned at the plaintiff's request, recourse to Rule 3 was legally impermissible. The ratio squarely governs the present controversy. Here too, the penultimate adjournment resulted from a strike by the legal fraternity and not from any request attributable to the appellants.

The above principle finds reaffirmation in Muhammad Aslam v. Nazir Ahmed (2008 SCMR 942) wherein this Court explained that Order XVII Rule 3 does not authorise dismissal of the suit merely because evidence is not produced on a particular date. Rather, the Court is required to proceed in accordance with law and, where the party is present, must not deprive it of the opportunity of appearing in the witness box. The Court further held that the expression "proceed to decide the suit forthwith" cannot be equated with an automatic dismissal of the suit.

Likewise, in Syed Tahir Hussain Mehmoodi v. Agha Syed Liaqat Ali (2014 SCMR 637), this Court reiterated that Order XVII Rule 3 is a penal provision which must be strictly construed and can only be applied where the case squarely falls within its mischief. In the present case, however, the statutory conditions for invoking the provision were never satisfied because the adjournment immediately preceding the impugned order was neither sought nor occasioned by the appellants.

The respondents' emphasis upon the number of opportunities granted also does not advance their case. As explained by this Court in Rana Tanveer Khan v. Naseer-ud-Din (2015 SCMR 1401), the decisive consideration is not merely the number of adjournments but whether those opportunities had been availed at the request of the party and whether the case had truly fallen within the mischief of Order XVII Rule 3. CPC. The facts before us are materially distinguishable, for the impugned order followed an adjournment necessitated by a lawyers' strike rather than by any default attributable to the appellants.

We are equally unable to agree with the view taken by the Courts below that the review petition was incompetent merely because the impugned order was appealable. Undoubtedly, an appeal lay against the order dated 14.10.2009. Equally true, however, is that the appellants elected to seek review before invoking the appellate jurisdiction. Although an appeal lay against the order dated 14.10.2009, the existence of an appellate remedy did not ipso facto exclude the review jurisdiction where the order suffered from an error apparent on the face of the record. The doctrine of election merely requires a litigant to choose between concurrent remedies; it does not render the chosen remedy inherently incompetent where the law otherwise permits its invocation.

The order dated 14.10.2009, having been passed by invoking a jurisdiction plainly unavailable in the circumstances of the case, suffered from an error apparent on the face of the record. The illegality was self-evident from the order sheets themselves which disclosed that the immediately preceding adjournment had not been granted on the request of the appellants. Such an error fell squarely within the limited scope of review jurisdiction1. Recently, in Gul Tiaz Khan Marwat v. Registrar, Peshawar High Court (2026 SCMR 287), this Court reiterated that review lies where the decision is per incuriam or where the error is so manifest that it floats on the surface of the record and materially affects the outcome of the case.

Accordingly, the learned trial Court erred in dismissing the review petition solely on the premise that the original order was appealable. Since the impugned order itself was patently without lawful authority and disclosed an error apparent on the face of the record, the review petition was competent and deserved adjudication on its merits rather than rejection on a technical ground. For the foregoing reasons, the foundation upon which the trial Court dismissed the suit and the subsequent Courts sustained that course of action cannot be legally maintained. The impugned orders, therefore, call for interference.

As an upshot of the foregoing discussion, this appeal is allowed. The order dated 14.10.2009, whereby the learned trial Court invoked the provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C. and closed the appellants' right to adduce evidence, is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is, accordingly, set aside. Consequently, the subsequent order of the learned trial Court dismissing the review petition, the judgment of the learned Appellate Court affirming the said orders, as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court, are also set aside. The matter is remanded to the learned trial Court, which shall restore the suit to its original number, afford the appellants a reasonable opportunity to adduce their evidence, permit the respondents to lead evidence in rebuttal, 1 Government of Punjab v. Aamir Zahoor ul Haq (PLD 2016 Supreme Court 421) and Nadia Naz v. The President of Islamic Republic of Pakistan (PLD 2023 Supreme Court 588) if so advised, and thereafter decide the suit afresh strictly in accordance with law, uninfluenced by any observation made herein touching upon the merits of the controversy. Considering that the litigation has remained pending for an inordinately long period, the learned trial Court shall endeavour to conclude the proceedings and render its judgment within a period of six months from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this judgment, even if it has to fix the case on day-to-day basis.

Before parting with this judgement, we consider it appropriate to advert to certain systemic concerns which this litigation has brought into sharp focus. The present case is a classic illustration of the distinction between the existence of judicial discretion and its sound exercise. A perusal of the order sheets reveals that the learned trial Court had, on several earlier occasions, before it, instances where the delay in the proceedings was genuinely attributable to the conduct of the plaintiffs. Had the learned trial Court considered that the repeated defaults had reached a stage warranting invocation of the penal provisions of Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C., it could have exercised such jurisdiction on one of those occasions, subject always to the fulfilment of the statutory requirements. Curiously, however, the provision was invoked on the one date when the preceding adjournment had not been granted at the request of the plaintiffs at all, but had resulted from a strike observed by the legal fraternity. Thus, while the trial Court possessed the discretion to invoke Order XVII Rule 3, CPC, in an appropriate case, its exercise in the facts obtaining on 14.10.2009 was contrary to law. Judicial discretion is not an unfettered licence; it is a legal trust to be exercised on sound principles, consistent with the statute and the facts of the case. An order passed in disregard of the conditions prescribed by law ceases to be an exercise of discretion and becomes an arbitrary exercise of power.

This case also compels us to express our deep concern over the growing culture of unwarranted adjournments which continues to plague the administration of civil justice. Members of the Bar undoubtedly shoulder demanding professional commitments and frequently appear before multiple fora on the same day. Nevertheless, every advocate owes an overriding duty to the client, to the Court and to the administration of justice. Once a counsel accepts a brief, it is incumbent upon him to ensure that the matter is properly attended to, particularly where important proceedings, such as recording of evidence, are scheduled. The routine plea that learned counsel is engaged before a superior Court cannot, by itself, constitute sufficient cause. Superior Courts ordinarily conclude substantial judicial work well before the close of the working day, leaving adequate time for counsel to honour commitments undertaken before subordinate Courts. Trial Courts ordinarily function throughout the working day, and, in the ordinary course, there exists sufficient opportunity for counsel to attend proceedings before subordinate Courts after conclusion of matters in the superior Courts. More fundamentally, an advocate should accept only such number of briefs as can reasonably be discharged with competence, diligence and fidelity to the client's cause. Professional overcommitment cannot be permitted to become a justification for repeated disruption of judicial proceedings.

The unfortunate consequence of this practice is seldom borne by the defaulting advocate. More often than not, it is the litigant who is admonished in open Court for the absence of counsel, or a junior associate, having no meaningful instructions and no effective control over the conduct of the case, is left to face the displeasure of the Court. Such a practice neither serves the interest of justice nor enhances public confidence in the legal profession. Every advocate is an officer of the Court, and the obligations attached to that office require punctuality, preparedness and respect for the Court's time as much as they require loyalty to the client.

The responsibility, however, does not rest with the Bar alone. Trial Courts are equally entrusted with maintaining discipline in judicial proceedings and must adhere to the provisions of Order XVII, Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which permit the adjournment of a case only where ‘sufficient cause’ is shown. It has become increasingly common to find orders successively recording "last opportunity", followed by "final opportunity", and thereafter yet another "last and final opportunity". Such repeated indulgence reduces solemn judicial directions to empty formalities and inevitably erodes the authority and sanctity of the Court's own orders. A judicial order describing an opportunity as the "last" must ordinarily mean precisely that. If the Court itself repeatedly dilutes its own directions, litigants inevitably begin to treat judicial orders as negotiable rather than mandatory. If the Court genuinely considers that the default warrants the consequences contemplated by law, it should not hesitate to invoke the relevant statutory provision, including Order XVII Rule 3, C.P.C., where its conditions are satisfied. Conversely, at the cost of repetition, where justice requires further indulgence, the Court must record reasons for extending time and impose realistic and deterrent costs commensurate with the inconvenience caused to the opposite party and the burden placed upon the justice system. Nominal costs, imposed merely as a matter of routine, have ceased to serve any meaningful deterrent purpose.

The ultimate responsibility for ensuring orderly conduct of proceedings rests upon the Judges while sitting in Court during Court hours and is not left to the convenience of the litigants or their counsel2. A trial Judge is expected to regulate the progress of the case with firmness, fairness and consistency, ensuring that judicial orders command respect and that proceedings are not allowed to drift through repeated and unjustified adjournments. Equally, it is unsettling to observe the growing tendency of counsel to seek yet another adjournment despite earlier orders expressly recording that the opportunity granted would be the "last", "final" or “absolute final” one. Such requests ought not to be made as a matter of course, for they undermine the authority of the Court and encourage the perception that judicial directions are negotiable rather than binding. Respect for the rule of law begins with respect for the orders of the Court, and both the Bench and the Bar share an equal responsibility to ensure that the administration of justice is conducted with discipline, efficiency and faithfulness to the law. Stepping further, every segment of society has a collective responsibility to contribute towards the development of a just, 2 O. XVII, Rule 1, CPC harmonious, and progressive social order, worthy of its people. Such an objective can only be grasped and developed through observance of moral values, mutual respect, and a spirit of tolerance, rather than by yielding to personal gains. Personal vendetta when allowed to surpass reason and civility, not only weakens the threads that unite individuals within society but also destabilizes the moral fabric of the nation, ultimately contributing to its institutional and social decay; therefore, when a counsel makes professional commitments, he has to fulfill the same timely so as to augment the trust of the individual(s) on the institution(s) and not to linger on the matter only for worldly gains.

Lastly, we consider that the observations made herein in paragraphs 17 to 21 concern an issue of systemic importance touching upon judicial case management, professional responsibility of the Bar, and the effective administration of civil justice. Accordingly, the Office is directed to transmit copies of this judgment to the Hon'ble Chief Justices of all the High Courts for circulation amongst the Judicial Officers subordinate to their respective Courts, and to the Provincial Bar Councils, as well as the Islamabad Bar Council, for dissemination amongst members of the Bar, so that due regard may be made to the observations made hereinabove while conducting and regulating civil proceedings in Courts across the country. JUDGE JUDGE Lahore, the 03rd of August, 2026 “Approved for Reporting” M.A. Hassan
